newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo banks seek delay in bank law implementation.
newsitem.headline: Yugo banks seek delay in bank law implementation.

text.p: Yugoslavia's banks cautioned on Tuesday they could face closures if the government decides to fully implement from June 30 the law on banks, setting strict criteria for the industry.

Bankers said they could not meet nine criteria set by the law and appealed to the National Bank of Yugoslavia (NBY) and the federal Finance Ministry to postpone implementation of the law for two years promising they would improve their position.
Yugoslav Banking Association (YBA) said it had appealed to the NBY to delay implementation of the law on banks, especially criteria which banks must meet to preserve their licences.
"If all criteria were implemented Yugoslav banks would cease to exist," YBA General Secretary Mileta Babovic said.

"YBA failed to get a positive response from the NBY and the Finance Ministry who said there was no more reason to delay the implementation of the law because banks themselves did nothing to improve their position," Babovic said.

To retain their licences, banks must meet an 8.00 percent capital adequacy ratio, have capital equalling at least 20 percent of their liabilities, while 50 percent of their liabilities must be generated from individuals' deposits.
Short-term lending and short-term sources of finance must be 100-percent matched. Hard currency liabilities and assets ratio cannot be lower than 95 percent or higher than 105 percent.

The largest credit extended cannot exceed 80 percent of the bank's capital. Permanent investment in companies is set at 15 percent and in banks and other financial institutions at 51 percent. Investment in fixed assets cannot exceed 20 percent.
Milos Milosavljevic, managing director of Jugobanka, insisted the NBY announcement was misinterpreted and that the central bank will only start to analyse positions of individual banks from June 30.

"Can you imagine how it would sound to the international audience to hear the news that Yugoslav banks have dissapeared? Those who make such decisions must take full responsibility for them," he said.

"We have definitely done nothing to improve our position as banks, but if we seek another delay in implementing the law to the full, we must also envisage a gradual approach to improve our position," he added.
Milosavljevic, also a president of the YBA Executive Board, said bankers could not demand a simple two year delay again without promising to meet those criteria step-by-step.
Bankers said they expected the situation in the financial sector to improve over the last two years, but instead, their problems remained unchanged.

"First, we have expected banks balances to be cleared from frozen savings and that Yugoslavia will reopen talks with its external creditors. But this has not happened and the economy performed under extreme illiquidity and that is why we failed to meet expectations," Babovic said. -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
